365.title: The self is dearer than a son (1.4)
365.hook: a line that sounds selfish until you see which self it means
365.tomorrow: Yajnavalkya and his two wives: he's leaving
365.howItsDone: Teachers of Vedanta use this passage to explain that the atman, not the ego, is the source of all love; it is read alongside Yajnavalkya's teaching to Maitreyi later in the same Upanishad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ardha: the self split in two, and the two halves chased each other down to the ants. Your line was you are the half.

Three hundred sixty-five. One day at a time, that's a whole calendar year on this path. Now a question that sounds like a trap. Ask a parent: who do you love more, your child or yourself? The answer may come before the question ends. My child. Obviously. Yet the Brihadaranyaka says, flatly, the self is dearer than a son. It sounds selfish. It sounds wrong. Stay with it, because the whole line turns on one small Sanskrit word.
screen: `A WHOLE YEAR OF DAYS.` → `YOUR CHILD OR YOURSELF?` → `THE SELF IS DEARER THAN A SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the line in full. This self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else, because it is more inward. That's the small word: antaratara, more inner, closer in. One way to read it: the text isn't measuring how much anyone loves. It's asking where love lives. When you love your child, where is that love felt? Not in the child. In you, from the inside. The self here isn't your ego, your reputation, your wants. Two days ago we met aham asmi, I am, before any name, and Vedanta readers hear that self here: the one at the center, the place every love is felt from. Then the text adds a warning. If someone calls anything else most dear, and another person tells them, you'll lose what you love, it may well come true. A son can be lost. Wealth can be lost. So, the text says, hold the self alone as dear, and what you hold dear won't perish. The schools of Vedanta read this self in different ways. Advaita hears the one self that is also the self of your son, so loving it leaves nobody out. Devotional schools hear the soul, whose own inner self is God. Neither hears permission to love a child less. A conversation later in this book makes the same point about a husband and a wife. On this reading, love isn't only aimed outward. It's lit from the inside, and the text calls that inside the one dear thing that won't perish.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love without effort: a child, a parent, a friend, a pet, and let the feeling come. Then, gently, notice where you're feeling it from: not where they are, but here, in you. Rest in that warm center, and notice it was there before they came to mind, and is still there now.
Priya, dear, beloved. Dearer than wealth, dearer than all else, the Brihadaranyaka says, because it is more inward.
Your line: love the self. Tomorrow, a husband says he's leaving. Three hundred sixty-five days, a whole year.

366.title: Yajnavalkya and his two wives: he's leaving (2.4)
366.hook: the greatest sage in the book tells his wife he's leaving home for good, and offers to split the property
366.tomorrow: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?"
366.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition sannyasa is taken by formal vows, often late in life, after which the renunciant leaves home and property behind; the four stages of life are an ideal pattern described in the dharma texts, and the householder's life is honored in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, priya: the self is dearer than a son, because it is more inward. Your line was love the self.

A kitchen, a long marriage, an ordinary evening. And the husband says: I'm going. Not to another house. Not to another person. He's leaving the householder's life altogether, to wander with nothing. Before I go, he says, let me divide what I have between you and my other wife, so it's settled. So begins one of the Brihadaranyaka's great conversations. The man is Yajnavalkya, and today is about what it meant, in his world, to leave.
screen: `I'M GOING.` → `NOT TO ANOTHER HOUSE.` → `LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya is a leading voice of this Upanishad. Tradition credits him with a whole branch of the Veda, the White Yajurveda, and in a few days you'll watch him take on a room full of rivals. Here he's at home, with two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani. That's nearly all this chapter tells us about them. When the scene is told again later in the book, it adds one line: Maitreyi was one who discussed Brahman, and Katyayani had, in the text's short phrase, a woman's knowledge, words readers interpret in different ways. The text never tells us what Katyayani thought, or how either of them felt, and it's fair to say so. Why is he leaving? Hindu tradition later described life in four stages: the student, the householder, the forest dweller, and the renunciant, the sannyasi, who gives up home, property and name, and wanders. Yajnavalkya is stepping from the second stage toward the last. In the retelling, the verb is the one used for going forth into that wandering life. And notice what he does first. He doesn't vanish in the night. He sits down and tries to settle the property fairly. Even leaving everything, he wants to leave well. This whole conversation appears twice in the Brihadaranyaka, in book two and again in book four, with small differences, and the book keeps both tellings. What keeps the scene alive is what Maitreyi says next.
screen: `A LEADING VOICE OF THIS UPANISHAD.` · `TWO WIVES; THE TEXT SAYS LITTLE MORE.` · `FROM HOUSEHOLDER TO WANDERER.` · `TOLD TWICE IN THE SAME BOOK.` · then, large: `THE MAN WHO LEFT.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're getting ready to leave, or will one day: a job, a house, a role, a habit, a stage of life. Don't decide anything; just ask what Yajnavalkya asked: what would it take to settle this fairly, so the people around it are cared for? Let one small answer come, then let the question go and rest with the breath.
Sannyasa, renunciation, laying everything down. He is leaving home for good, and first offers to settle his property between Maitreyi and Katyayani.
Your line: the man who left. Tomorrow, Maitreyi answers him with a question. See you then.

367.title: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?" (2.4)
367.hook: offered her share of the property, Maitreyi asks the one question that makes the settlement worthless
367.tomorrow: "the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on"
367.howItsDone: Maitreyi is remembered across Hindu tradition as a woman philosopher who chose knowledge over wealth; teachers of Vedanta often begin with her question when explaining why the Upanishads seek the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sannyasa: Yajnavalkya was going forth to wander, and offered to settle his property first. Your line was the man who left.

Papers on the table. Everything divided, fair and square. Sign here. And instead of signing, Maitreyi asks a question. Sir, if this whole earth, full of wealth, belonged to me, would that make me immortal? Yajnavalkya is an honest man. No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich, but there's no hope of deathlessness through wealth. Then she says the line this day is named for.
screen: `SIGN HERE.` → `WOULD THE WHOLE EARTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `NO.`

segments.voice: What would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. She doesn't refuse the money in a temper, and she doesn't make a speech about it. She sees that the settlement answers the wrong question, and asks for the right one. Notice the word she uses: amrita, deathless, the same word as the nectar the gods churned from the ocean. She wants the thing that doesn't end. And Yajnavalkya is delighted. You were always dear to me, he says, and now you say what's dear. Come, sit. I'll explain it to you, and as I do, reflect on it. His first words are strange. Truly, it is not for the husband's sake that a husband is dear. Not for the wife's sake that a wife is dear. Not for the sons' sake that sons are dear. Not for wealth's sake that wealth is dear. And on: not for the gods' sake are the gods dear, not for all beings' sake are all beings dear. Today, stay with the first half, the not. It isn't cold. It's taking apart a habit. It's easy to think love is only about the other person, a thing out there that pulls. Yajnavalkya says: look again. Something in the love isn't about them at all. Tomorrow, the second half of the sentence, the part that says what love is for.

368.title: "The self is to be seen, heard, reflected on" (2.4)
368.hook: the second half of Yajnavalkya's sentence, and the four verbs a whole school of philosophy is built on
368.carry: for the sake of the self
368.tomorrow: the lump of salt dissolved — no inside, no outside
368.howItsDone: In Vedanta study, students follow the three steps drawn from this verse: shravana, hearing the teaching from a teacher; manana, reflecting on it and resolving doubts; and nididhyasana, sustained contemplation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maitreyi set aside the whole earth full of wealth and asked for what doesn't die, and Yajnavalkya began: not for the husband's sake is a husband dear.

Try catching a drumbeat. Not the drum: the sound. Reach into the air after it's struck and grab the boom. You can't. It's gone before your hand closes. But put your hand on the drum, or on the drummer's arm, and the sound is in your hands. Yajnavalkya uses that picture in the middle of his talk with Maitreyi. Today he finishes yesterday's sentence, and tells her where to put her hand.
screen: `TRY CATCHING A DRUMBEAT.` → `HOLD THE DRUM INSTEAD.` → `WHERE TO PUT YOUR HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sentence. Not for the husband's sake is a husband dear, but for the sake of the self a husband is dear. Not for the wife's sake, but for the sake of the self. And so on through sons, wealth, gods, all beings, everything. Then the line this day is named for: atma va are drashtavyah shrotavyo mantavyo nididhyasitavyah. The self, my dear, is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected on, to be meditated on, Maitreyi. And when the self is seen, heard, reflected on and understood, all this is known. That's where the drum comes in. You can't catch the sounds one by one. Hold the drum, or the drummer, and the sounds are held. He gives two more: the conch, and the vina, a stringed instrument. Know the source, and you know what comes from it. Later teachers of Vedanta, Shankara among them, built a method on these four verbs. Shravana: hearing the teaching, really listening. Manana: reflecting, turning it over, answering your own doubts. Nididhyasana: dwelling in it, steadily, until it's not an idea any more. And seeing, which comes first in the sentence, Shankara's school reads as the goal, the thing the other three are for. Listen first. Think second. Sit with it third.

segments.voice: Hear: say the line quietly to yourself once, for the sake of the self. Reflect: let one question about it come, and turn it over for a few breaths without forcing an answer. Then dwell: drop the words and rest where they were pointing, and when thoughts come back, start again at hearing.
Nididhyasana, steady contemplation. The last of the four ways to know the self, when the teaching stops being an idea and starts being lived.

369.title: The lump of salt dissolved — no inside, no outside (2.4)
369.hook: Yajnavalkya drops salt in water, says there's no awareness after death, and Maitreyi says: now you've confused me
369.tomorrow: the honey doctrine — all beings are honey for each other
369.howItsDone: Teachers of Vedanta use the salt image, from both the Chandogya and the Brihadaranyaka, to explain how the self pervades everything; this passage is read and debated in Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita commentaries alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nididhyasana: the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on. Hear, reflect, dwell. Your line was for the sake of the self.

A lump of salt, dropped into water overnight. In the morning it's gone, yet every sip is salty, here, and here. Twenty days ago, in the Chandogya, a father used that salt to teach his son. Today, in a different book, a different teacher picks it up: Yajnavalkya, still talking with Maitreyi. And this time the salt says something she can't follow. She tells him so, out loud. Here, sir, you've confused me.
screen: `SALT IN WATER, AGAIN.` → `A DIFFERENT TEACHER.` → `HERE, SIR, YOU'VE CONFUSED ME.`

segments.voice: As a lump of salt thrown into water dissolves, he says, and you can't pick it out again, but wherever you take the water from it's salty, so this great being, endless, without limit, is nothing but a mass of knowing. It rises up out of these elements, and vanishes back into them. Then the hard line: after death, there is no awareness. Maitreyi stops him. That's where you've confused me. She's not slow. It sounds as if the deathless self she asked for just dissolved into nothing. Yajnavalkya says: I'm saying nothing confusing. Listen. Where there seems to be two, one sees another, hears another, knows another. But where everything has become one's own self, then by what, and whom, would one see? By what would one know the knower? So the salt isn't gone. It's everywhere. What ends is the gap between a knower and something known. When the scene is told again later in the book, the salt image grows sharper, and gives today its title: a lump of salt has no inside and no outside; it's taste all the way through. So this self has no inside, no outside; it's knowing all the way through. Schools of Vedanta read the dissolving differently. For Advaita, the separate knower melts like the salt, and only pure consciousness is left. Other schools read that line, no awareness after death, as the end of the narrow, body-bound kind of knowing, not of the soul itself. Neither reading turns the self into nothing. Maitreyi's confusion is the right question, asked out loud.

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you: a car, a fan, your own breath. When a thought builds the wall again, me in here, the world out there, let it dissolve like the salt.

370.title: The honey doctrine — all beings are honey for each other (2.5)
370.hook: a secret teaching, once passed on by a sage with a horse's head: everything is honey for everything else
370.tomorrow: Janaka's court: the thousand cows with gold horns
370.howItsDone: The honey doctrine, madhu vidya, is studied as a meditation in the Vedanta tradition; ayam atma brahma, this self is Brahman, from its closing lines and from the Mandukya Upanishad, is counted among the great sayings, the mahavakyas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vijnanaghana: like dissolved salt, no inside, no outside, knowing all the way through. Your line was pure consciousness.

Old Vedic stories tell of a sage named Dadhyanc who knew a secret teaching called the honey knowledge. The god Indra, the stories say, warned him: teach it to anyone, and I'll cut off your head. Two divine twins, the Ashvins, wanted it badly. So they took off his head, gave him a horse's head, and he taught them through that. Indra struck it off, and the twins put his own head back. The Brihadaranyaka quotes old hymns that remember the horse-headed teacher, and gives us the teaching itself, the one worth risking a head for.

segments.voice: This earth, it says, is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth. Madhu: honey, sweetness, the thing that feeds. The earth feeds every creature, and every creature feeds the earth back. Then the same line, again and again, like a chant. Water is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for water. Fire. Wind. The sun. The directions. The moon. Lightning. Thunder. Space. Dharma. Truth. Humankind. And last, the self. And each time the text adds: the shining, deathless person in that thing, and the shining, deathless person in you, are just this self. That's the secret. Not a chain with a top and a bottom, but everything feeding everything, because the same self lives in both. Then a picture: as the spokes of a wheel are all held in the hub and the rim, so all beings, all gods, all worlds are held in this self. And near the end of the chapter, three short words that later teachers count among the great sayings of the Upanishads: ayam atma brahma. This self is Brahman. Earlier, in the Chandogya, the bees gathered honey from many trees, and no drop could say which tree it came from. That was about losing your separate name. This is about something else: every being is honey too, feeding and being fed at once.
screen: `THE EARTH IS HONEY FOR ALL BEINGS.` · `AGAIN AND AGAIN, THE SAME SHAPE.` · `SPOKES HELD IN THE HUB.` · `AYAM ATMA BRAHMA.` · then, large: `MADHU.`

segments.voice: Name one thing that fed you today: food, water, sunlight, someone's patience, and let it be sweet. Then turn it around and name one way you fed something back: the plant you watered, the friend you answered, the earth your breath went out to. Go gently back and forth, fed by, feeding, and let the line in the text become a rhythm.
Madhu, honey, sweetness. The thing every being is for every other: the earth for us, and us for the earth.
Your line: everything feeding everything. Tomorrow, a thousand cows with gold on their horns. Until then.

371.title: Janaka's court: the thousand cows with gold horns (3.1)
371.hook: a king offers a thousand gold-horned cows to the wisest person in the room, and only one man dares to take them
371.tomorrow: Ashvala asks about death and ritual
371.howItsDone: The debate in Janaka's court, the third book of the Brihadaranyaka, is studied in Vedanta as a series of short dialogues; Hindu tradition remembers Janaka as a model of the king who lives among riches without clinging to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the honey doctrine: the earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for the earth. Your line was everything feeding everything.

A royal courtyard, crowded with learned priests from the Kuru and Panchala lands. In the middle, penned together, a thousand cows. On the horns of every one, the text says, gold is tied. King Janaka stands up. Honored scholars, he says, whoever among you is wisest in Brahman, drive these cows home. The room goes silent. Nobody moves. Taking the cows means claiming to be the wisest person there, and every other priest will come for you.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS. GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `WHOEVER IS WISEST, TAKE THEM.` → `NOBODY MOVES.`

segments.voice: Then Yajnavalkya turns to his own student. Samashravas, my dear, he says, drive them home. And the student does. The room explodes. How can he call himself the wisest among us? The king's own hotri priest, Ashvala, steps up. Yajnavalkya, are you really the wisest among us? And Yajnavalkya answers. We bow to the wisest. We just want the cows. It's funny, and it's sly. He claims nothing, and he'll answer any question you've got. That sets up the whole third book of the Brihadaranyaka: a day of debate. One after another, challengers step forward, one of them twice, each with the hardest question they have. Over the next ten days we'll take them one at a time. And a word about the king. Janaka of Videha appears again and again in these texts as a king hungry for teaching. Sita's father in the Ramayana is also called Janaka, king of Videha. Janaka may have been a name several kings of Videha carried, and nobody can say for sure whether these are the same man. Look back at this week: priya. The man who left. Maitreyi setting aside the earth. Seen, heard, reflected on. Salt with no inside or outside. Honey for each other. And now a room full of cows, and a question that could cost someone everything.
screen: `DRIVE THEM HOME, MY DEAR.` · `WE BOW TO THE WISEST.` · `WE JUST WANT THE COWS.` · `CHALLENGERS, ONE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `WHO IS THE WISEST?`

segments.voice: If a memory comes, recall a time you stayed quiet in a room because speaking up meant being judged: a meeting, a class, a family dinner. Don't relive it; just notice how it felt in the body. Then bring to mind Yajnavalkya's ease, we bow to the wisest, and let some of it into your shoulders as you breathe.
Janaka's court. Where a king asked for the brahmishtha, the one most wise in Brahman: the title nobody there dared to claim, and Yajnavalkya never quite claimed either.
Your line: who is the wisest? Tomorrow, the first challenger, a priest, steps up. Day three hundred seventy-one, done.
